options.author: first read (Wonder)
options.case: This is a study in social plausibility: Tatsuya wins not despite being charming but because charm, rank, flattery and appetite are indistinguishable in the world he moves through. The horror is that his predation has no special register. It sounds like energy, competence, even good humour, until the reader hears what it is counting. He ingratiates himself with the inn maids, Zenpei, Mitsuyo’s whole household, and finally with officials, while privately treating a government coal-mine disposal as plunder and Mitsuyo as part of the payment. Zenpei is not simply deceived: his vanity and greed make him enjoy being deceived. Tsunao sees Tatsuya at once, but rectitude without social grace looks pale, pedantic and ungenerous beside him. For the English: Keep the story’s surface genuinely charming. Tatsuya must work in English as he works in a room—quick, amusing, at ease—and then, alone, reveal himself in the same untroubled voice: Mitsuyo is “beautiful prey,” her father is to be hooked, his debts and the mining concession are parts of one campaign. Do not signal villainy in advance, do not make the soliloquy brooding or conscience-stricken, and do not soften its sporting delight. The shock depends on how little his tone changes.
options.tradeoff: Makes the exposure a matter of content overheard in an unchanged, socially plausible voice, so charm itself becomes the horror.

options.author: crux check (Wonder)
options.case:
The story is told in a high, lyrical, scenic narration that never lowers itself to judge its villain, while the moral exposure happens entirely through a split in Tatsuya's voice. The hot-spring landscape, lake, and seasonal close are rendered in ornate, impersonal periods (p2-p4, p37, p40), and the same surface covers a corrupt mining concession. Tatsuya is all polished deference with Zenpei and hosts (p7, p101-p112), but alone he becomes 'ore': Mitsuyo is a 'beautiful prize' (美しき獲物, p16), Tsunao is to be crushed 'konagona' (p48), and the mine, the father, and the girl are one rapid campaign — '兵は神速' (p49). Mitsuyo, by contrast, is characterised by unvaried insistence and repetition — 真実に six times in one outburst (p27) — which Zenpei then mocks by repetition back. Flatten any of this into uniformly fluent, psychologically explanatory English and Tatsuya becomes either a declared cad or a romantic suitor, and Mitsuyo a merely charming ingenue, instead of the predator and the child the juxtaposition shows. For the English: Keep a distinctly elevated, periodic narrative prose, but let dialogue break register sharply: Mitsuyo's repetitions and girl's protests must stay repetitive rather than be varied for elegance, Zenpei's bluff familiarity stay bluff, and Tatsuya must sound ingratiating in company and coarsely proprietorial alone. Do not make Tatsuya slangy throughout, or Mitsuyo more articulate and knowing than she is.
- The ending, and the narration throughout, withholds the very facts a reader most wants — who got Mitsuyo, what the bribery came to, who was punished — and that withholding is the story's verdict. Tatsuya's demand is made brutally explicit — the reward for the draft cabinet order is Mitsuyo herself: 'お貰い申しましたよ' (p130) — and then the narrator simply stops: 'われはこの後のことを知らず' (p132). What follows is only rumour and rhetorical question: Tatsuya has taken a wife, 'その妻は誰なるらん'; someone has thrown himself into philosophy, 'その人は誰なるらん'; '明日は誰が身の'. Earlier the same reticence governs motive and perception (the singer identified only by inference, p10; Tsunao and Tatsuya each privately misreading the other while Zenpei alone imagines mutual respect, p44). For the English: Preserve every refusal to resolve: do not name the wife, do not identify the philosopher beyond what the syntax leaves open, do not add a concluding moral, a marriage, a ruin, or an ironic wink that settles it. English pronouns and connectives must be chosen to keep the same degree of knowing-and-not-knowing as the Japanese.
options.tradeoff: Makes the exposure a marked split of register against elevated narration, and adds the narrator's withholding of outcome as a second, governing crux.

fork.question: Do the readers name the same crux in different words, or different cruxes — in particular, does Tatsuya's predation speak in the same untroubled voice as his charm, or in a coarsely proprietorial voice split from it, and is the ending's refusal to resolve part of the crux or not?

data.reason: They do not name the same thing in different words. They agree that Tatsuya's charm carries his predation, but they contradict each other on the mechanism that a translation must reproduce: Option 0 stakes everything on how little his tone changes alone, while Option 1 stakes it on a sharp register split — polished deference in company, 'ore' and 'konagona' alone — set against elevated narration, and adds a second crux Option 0 never mentions, the narration's withholding of outcome. That difference will govern Tatsuya's voice on every page and the handling of the close, so being wrong would be expensive and the text as presented does not settle it for the desk.
data.say: The readers name overlapping material but different cruxes: Option 0 locates the horror in Tatsuya's unchanged voice, Option 1 in a register split plus withheld resolution, and those give opposite instructions for the English. I am opening a fork rather than merging them. Recommendation: proceed on Option 1 until you rule, because it alone ties its claim to checkable features of the text — the 'ore' soliloquy, the repetitions, 'われはこの後のことを知らず' — whereas Option 0's 'same untroubled voice' would have to override that pronoun and register evidence; but if you judge the split to be a matter of situation rather than of voice, Option 0's reading of social plausibility is the one to adopt whole. House log: Fork opened on whether the crux is Tatsuya's unchanged charming voice or a split register against elevated, withholding narration, proceeding on the crux check's version pending the editor's ruling.
